title: Diatribae Duae
author: Damasus I
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0105.stoa007.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Hilarius etiam Liberti lapsum bis memorat : pri- mo contra Constantium, ubi haec ait : Vertisti deinde usque ad Romam bellum tuum, eripuisti illinc episco- pum : Et, oh te miserum! qui nescio utrum majore im- pietate relegaveris, quam remiseris (d). Tum deinde in fragmentis, quo loco Romanum hunc pontificem sus- ceptam a se Sirmiensem fidem scribentem, aposta- tam vocat, atque anathemati dat, verba non affero, quae inferius opportuniori loco recitanda a me sunt.
passages.english: Hilary also mentions the fall of Liberius twice: first in [the book] against Constantius, where he says this: "Then you turned your war as far as Rome, you snatched the bishop away from there: and, oh wretch that you are! I do not know whether you banished him with greater impiety than you sent him back." Then afterwards in the Fragments, in the place where he calls this Roman pontiff, writing that he had accepted the Sirmian faith, an apostate, and gives him over to anathema; I do not quote the words, since they are to be recited by me below in a more fitting place.
passages.notes: The "(d)" is a footnote reference in the printed edition.

passages.original: Sirmiensem itaque, quam Liberius susceperat fidem, Hilarius, ut vides perfidiam vocat : at quae perfidia hoc loco Hilario est, Sirmiensis una, ut vidimus, contra Photinum fides est; hanc enim ille exsecratur, hanc cum Nicaena comparat, hanc ipsam Liberio exprobrat; eam itaque Liberius susce- perat, Hilario teste. Ad haec igitur minime advertit animum, qui prior Hilarii fragmenta in lucem protu- lit, vir doctissimus Nicolaus Faber, et si qui sunt alii, qui iis Hilarii verbis, secundam exprimi Sir- miensem formulam putant : an vero ille eam desi- guare hoc loco potuit, de qua neque cum haec scribe- ret, neque toto fragmentorum opere, aut agere un- quam, aut ne cogitare quidem visus est?
passages.english: So the Sirmian faith which Liberius had accepted Hilary, as you see, calls a perfidy; but the perfidy in this passage of Hilary is, as we have seen, solely the Sirmian faith against Photinus; for it is this that he execrates, this that he compares with the Nicene, this very [faith] that he reproaches Liberius with; this, therefore, is what Liberius had accepted, on Hilary's testimony. To these points, then, the most learned Nicolas Faber, who first brought the fragments of Hilary to light, paid no attention at all, nor did any others there may be who think that the second Sirmian formula is expressed by those words of Hilary. But could he really have designated in this passage that [formula] which, neither when he wrote these things nor in the whole work of the Fragments, he appears ever to have dealt with, or even thought of?

passages.original: Deinde, si recte advertas, fidei quam Liberius susceperat conscribendae, neque Hosium, neque Po- tamium, neque Germinium praesentes fuisse Hilarius ait. Cur vero eos reticuisset, si secundam Sirmien- sem formulam eo loco exagitaret, quam alibi ab iis conscriptam ait? Aliam itaque tunc designaverit, ne- cesse est, Sirmiensem scilicet editam contra Photi- num, cui nullus ex iis adfuit : contra vero Sirmien- si, quam Liberius susceperat, perfidiae conscribendae, Theodorum, Basilium, et Eudoxium, idem Hilarius adfuisse asserit : at, si de Sirmiensi secunda formula haec inlelligas, falsissima sunt;
passages.english: Next, if you pay proper attention, Hilary says that neither Hosius, nor Potamius, nor Germinius was present at the drafting of the faith which Liberius had accepted. But why would he have passed over them in silence, if in that place he were attacking the second Sirmian formula, which elsewhere he says was drafted by them? He must therefore have then meant another, namely the Sirmian [faith] issued against Photinus, at which none of them was present. On the other hand, Hilary asserts that Theodore, Basil and Eudoxius were present at the drafting of the Sirmian perfidy which Liberius had accepted; but if you understand this of the second Sirmian formula, it is utterly false;

passages.original: Deinde cum viderent tantum eum Athanasio animorum consensum, et pacem agitari, metu invidiaque anxii fuere, et quod tot epi- scopi cum Athanasio communionem foverent, et quod formidarent, ut quos ipsi deceperant, a se deficerent, et huic unanimitati, communionique sese adjungerent, neve quod futurum videbatur, de eorum haeresi ubique fa- mosa triumphus ageretur. Constantium itaque una omnes adivisse, atque illum contra Magnentium pro- perantem adversus Athanasium ira iterum inflam- masse scribit, idque malorum omnium quae deinde secuta sunt, initium fuit. Hilarius autem, ut quae tunc agitaverant consilia effectui darent, Sirmii illos convenisse, asserit (c) homines mente calidos, inge- nio subtiles, militia pertinaces, occasionem revolvendi ejus, quod Athanasii absolutione dissolutum fuerat, ju- dicii quaesivisse, scribens, ut mortuam de Athanasio ipso jam tempore quaestionem, et veritatis judicio con- sepultam, in publicam recordationem nova Photini causa excitaret.
passages.english: Then, when they saw such great agreement of minds with Athanasius, and peace being pursued, they were anxious with fear and envy, both because so many bishops cherished communion with Athanasius, and because they dreaded that those whom they themselves had deceived would desert them and join themselves to this unanimity and communion, and lest, as seemed likely to happen, a triumph should be celebrated over their heresy, notorious everywhere. He writes, therefore, that they all went together to Constantius, and, as he was hastening against Magnentius, inflamed him again with anger against Athanasius, and this was the beginning of all the evils that followed afterwards. Hilary, for his part, asserts that, in order to put into effect the plans they had then been devising, they met at Sirmium, men hot in mind, subtle in wit, stubborn in warfare, writing that they sought an occasion of reopening the judgment which had been dissolved by the acquittal of Athanasius, so that by the new case of Photinus they might rouse into public memory the question about Athanasius, already dead by the very passage of time and buried together by the judgment of truth.
passages.notes: "tantum eum Athanasio" read as "tantum cum Athanasio".

passages.original: Quaeri tamen hoc loco posset, cur nulla in Seleuciensi etiam synodo, cui imperator Orientales omnes adesse jus- serat, ejusdem mentio sit? An forte ab iis turbis abesse maluit? An potius inter illos centum et quin- que Homoeusianos ab Hilario (d) memoratos, sed fugitans jurgiorum fuit? Utrumque fieri facile potuit, siquidem Basilius Magnus sic ilium animo affectum scribit : Constantinopolis dudum habet Demophilum, ac de illo quidem simulacrum quoddam recta fidei, et pietatis ab omnibus advenientibus summo consensu jactatur; adeo ut etiam dissidentes civitatis partes coa- luerint in unum, atque ex vicinis nonnulli episcopi conjunctionem amplexi sint (e).
passages.english: It could, however, be asked at this point why there is no mention of him also at the synod of Seleucia, which the emperor had ordered all the Easterners to attend. Did he perhaps prefer to stay away from those disturbances? Or was he rather among those hundred and five Homoiousians mentioned by Hilary, but avoiding quarrels? Either could easily have happened, since Basil the Great writes that he was disposed in mind thus: "Constantinople has for some time had Demophilus, and about him indeed a certain semblance of right faith and piety is spread abroad with the greatest agreement by all who arrive; so much so that even the dissenting parts of the city have grown together into one, and some of the neighbouring bishops have embraced union [with him]."

passages.original: Sed et alia est causa, cur ea formula non synodi, aut episcoporum, sed uno tantum imperatoris nomine missa videri oporteat. Si enim Hosium excipias, caeteri quatuor, quos Hilarius illius auctores fuisse asserit, extra Ecclesiae communionem fueram : hoc saltem de Ursacio et Valente Galli episcopi certo statuerant (e). Quamobrem omni cum orthodoxis episcopis interdicto per canones litterarum commer- cio, non erat cur illis consueto more ac de rebus ad fidem pertinentibus Ariani illi scriberent;
passages.english: But there is also another reason why that formula ought to be regarded as sent not in the name of a synod or of bishops, but in the name of the emperor alone. For, if you except Hosius, the other four, whom Hilary asserts were its authors, were outside the communion of the Church: this at least the bishops of Gaul had definitely decreed concerning Ursacius and Valens. Therefore, since all exchange of letters with orthodox bishops had been forbidden by the canons, there was no reason why those Arians should write to them in the customary way and about matters pertaining to the faith;

passages.original: Ursacius ipse, Valens ac Germinius Constantio obsequi, Sir- miensem formulam ejurare, atque Ancyranam ecthe- sim, quae tunc promulgata est, profiteri coacti sunt. Hinc illis omnes nocendi nervi repente, ac praeter omnem exspectationem, succisi sunt. Rem narrant Hilarius, Socrates ac Sozomenus, qui con- suli possunt. An non vides aperta omnia, et plana, ac quod Hilarius ait, Gallos et Ancyranos episcopos uno prope eodemque tempore impietatem illam damnasse, ut verissimum sit?
passages.english: Ursacius himself, Valens and Germinius were compelled to comply with Constantius, to abjure the Sirmian formula, and to profess the Ancyran *ecthesis* [statement of faith], which was promulgated at that time. From this, all their sinews for doing harm were suddenly, and beyond all expectation, cut. Hilary, Socrates and Sozomen narrate the matter, and they can be consulted. Do you not see that everything is open and plain, and that what Hilary says, that the Gallic and the Ancyran bishops condemned that impiety at almost one and the same time, is perfectly true?

passages.original: Id vero minime necesse est, ut dica- mus, cum aliud abjicere sit, aliud vero damnare, at- que unum, haud alterum inferat. Rem vero se ipsa manifestam duobus allatis exemplis confirmare placet, altero ex Hilario, altero ex Arianorum penu producto. Hilarius itaque Gallicanos episcopos laudat, quod missam ex Sirmiensi oppido infidelis fidei impieta- tem, non modo non suscepissent, sed nuntiatam, si- gnificatamque damnassent (d). Acaciani vero in se- leucensi synodo homousium, et homoeusium velut voces sacris Scripturis incognitas simpliciter reji- ciunt, Ιχ£άλλο;αν.
passages.english: But it is not at all necessary for us to say this, since to reject is one thing and to condemn another, and the one does not imply the other. I am pleased, however, to confirm a matter evident in itself by two examples adduced, one from Hilary, the other drawn from the Arians' storehouse. Hilary, then, praises the Gallican bishops because they not only did not accept the impiety of the faithless faith sent from the town of Sirmium, but condemned it when it was announced and made known to them. The Acacians, on the other hand, at the synod of Seleucia simply reject homoousion and homoiousion as words unknown to the sacred Scriptures, ἐκβάλλομεν ["we cast out"].
passages.notes: The Greek is garbled by the scan ("Ιχ£άλλο;αν"); probably ἐκβάλλομεν, "we reject".

passages.original: Syxti martyris ei episcopi in via Appia in coemeterio Calixti sepultus dicitur. Vides itaque quam haec similia sint inter se, atque hinc intelligis, quam facile fieri possit, ut impostor, qui aequioribus et te- nebrarum plenis saeculis Acta illa scripsit, ex Eusebio papa, cujus alioquin gesta diu in obscuro jacuisse sci- mus, Eusebium presbyterum effecerit, ac nobis ob- truserit (a). Sane Gregorius nonus, qui Ecclesiam sancti Eusebii consecravit, minime nos edocet, an ille episcopus, an presbyter fuerit (b), ex quo con- jici potest, nihil illum habuisse certum, exploratum- que, ac rem in vado etiam tum haesisse, quae hoc sae- culo Damasiani carminis beneficio lucem accepisse visa est.
passages.english: ... is said to have been buried on the Via Appia in the cemetery of Callixtus [beside the body] of Sixtus, martyr and bishop. You see, then, how similar these things are to one another, and from this you understand how easily it could happen that the impostor who wrote those Acts in more [unlearned] centuries full of darkness made Eusebius the presbyter out of Eusebius the pope, whose deeds otherwise we know lay long in obscurity, and foisted him on us. Certainly Gregory IX, who consecrated the church of Saint Eusebius, does not at all inform us whether he was a bishop or a presbyter; from which it can be conjectured that he had nothing certain and ascertained, and that the matter was even then stuck in the shallows, which in this century seems to have received light by the benefit of the poem of Damasus.
passages.notes: The sentence begins mid-construction (continuing "juxta corpus S."). "ei" read as "et". "aequioribus" makes little sense; perhaps "iniquioribus" or similar, rendered loosely.

passages.original: At quid interea cum Athanasio? An Liberius ejus communionem retinuerat? Sic equidem puto : Aria- nos enim, antequam is in exsilium pelleretur, id unum voluisse constat, ut pontifex Athanasium damnaret : at de mutanda a Liberio fide, ac omit- tendo homousio ne verbum quidem. Legantur litterae ab eo ad imperatorem tunc scriptae, ac colloquium Mediolani habitum. Abiit itaque Beroeam in Thracia exsul ob unam retentam cum Athanasio communio- nem : postremo fractus ad Orientales scripsit, Sir- miensem se suscepisse fidem, atque Athanasium a sua communione amovisse, pacemque cum iis habere velle : id Valenti etiam et Ursacio significavit quam- quam ea epistola suspicione non vacet.
passages.english: But what in the meantime about Athanasius? Had Liberius retained communion with him? So indeed I think: for it is established that the Arians, before he was driven into exile, wanted only this one thing, that the pontiff should condemn Athanasius; but about Liberius changing his faith and omitting the homoousion, not a word. Let the letters he wrote to the emperor at that time be read, and the conversation held at Milan. So he went off into exile to Beroea in Thrace solely because he had retained communion with Athanasius; at last, broken, he wrote to the Easterners that he had accepted the Sirmian faith, had removed Athanasius from his communion, and wished to have peace with them; he made this known also to Valens and Ursacius, although that letter is not free of suspicion.

passages.original: Caeterum, si quo tempore Ecclesiastica communio inter utrumque abrupta est, quin haec haud diu post- ea redintegrata fuerit, vix dubitaverit, qui legat ejusdem Athanasii epistolam ad episcopos AEgypti et Libyae, sive orationem primam contra Arianos, videatque eo loco Liberium atque Hosium inter Or- thodoxos episcopos, et fidei defensores laudatos (a). Haec enim cum scripta sit, ut Athanasius ait, anno a Nicaena synodo trigesimo sexto, validissimum aut numquam abruptae aut jam redintegratae charitatis argumentum praestat; si enim rationes subducas, annus tunc labebatur 360; si vero annos illos exac- tos jam esse vis, annus tibi 361 occurrit.
passages.english: Moreover, if at some time ecclesiastical communion between the two was broken off, hardly anyone will doubt that it was restored not long afterwards who reads the letter of the same Athanasius to the bishops of Egypt and Libya, or the first oration against the Arians, and sees Liberius and Hosius praised in that place among the orthodox bishops and defenders of the faith. For since this was written, as Athanasius says, in the thirty-sixth year from the synod of Nicaea, it furnishes a very strong argument of a charity either never broken off or already restored; for if you work out the reckoning, the year then running was 360; but if you would have those years already completed, you arrive at the year 361.

passages.original: quod erudite probat Bacchinius in dissertatione de Ecclesiasticae hierarchiae originibus (b), aperto Eu- sebii testimonio concilium a Cornelio in causa Novatiani ex tota qua patet Italia collectum, Ro- manum compellantis : at ne longe a Damasi aetate abeamus, Julius a sua synodo ad Eusebianos scri- bens : Necesse est, inquit, vobis notum facere etiamsi solus scripserim, non ideo mei solius, sed omnium eorum, qui in ITALIAsunt, et qui in his partibus degunt, esse illam sententiam (c). Liberius praeterea in litteris ad Orientales scriptis, quas Socrates recitat (d), episcopum se Italiae vocat, unusque Italorum atque Occidentalium ore loquitur : ac Theodoretus Romanam primam sub Damaso synodum ex Italia et Gallia collectam dicit (e). Consulatur, etiam P. Antonius Blancus, ex Obser- vantium familia vir doctus, qui hanc adversus Jannonii deliria sententiam egregie confirmat (f).
passages.english: as Bacchini learnedly proves in his dissertation on the origins of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, from the plain testimony of Eusebius, who calls Roman the council gathered by Cornelius in the case of Novatian from the whole extent of Italy. But, so as not to depart far from the age of Damasus, Julius, writing from his synod to the Eusebians, says: "It is necessary to make known to you that, even if I alone have written, that judgement is not on that account mine alone, but that of all those who are in Italy and who live in these parts." Liberius, moreover, in the letter written to the Easterners, which Socrates quotes, calls himself bishop of Italy, and speaks with the one voice of the Italians and the Westerners; and Theodoret says that the first Roman synod under Damasus was gathered from Italy and Gaul. P. Antonius Blancus, a learned man of the Observant family, may also be consulted, who excellently confirms this view against the ravings of Jannonius.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence. Letters in parentheses (b)–(f) are footnote marks and have been omitted. "Jannonius" not securely identified (possibly Pietro Giannone).

passages.original: Hinc cum Hieronymus (g) ex male intellecto Eusebii loco Romanam ab Italica diversam synodum, ubi de Cornelio agit, agnovisse visus sit, Pearsonus merito observat de hac Ita- lica synodo non liquere, ac dubitare se ait, an Italicum concilium illud ab Hieronymo recte con- flatum sit (h).
passages.english: Hence, since Jerome (g), from a misunderstood passage of Eusebius, seems to have recognized, where he treats of Cornelius, an Italian synod distinct from the Roman one, Pearson rightly observes that the matter of this Italian synod is not clear, and says that he doubts whether that Italian council was correctly constructed by Jerome (h).
passages.notes: The letters (g) and (h) are footnote marks from the printed edition.

passages.original: cujus (Nectarii) ordinatio, quem ordinem habuerit, non videmus. Contra vero quanta rerum copia, quanta verborum elegantia, cum sententiarum gravitate conjuncta in iis litteris, quas hac ipsa de causa Aquileiensis concilii nomine Ambrosius vere Theodosio scripsit! Utramque ipse, inter se conferat lector, ac suo ipse judicio censeat, in utraque ab eadem manu prolecta videri possit. Quid tandem, quod auctor Italicae hujus epistolae pactum, quod Meletium inter, et Paulinum juratum fuerat, quodve concordiam reddiderat Antiochenae Ecclesiae, Ignorare videtur, cum tamen illud Ambro- sio perspectum optime esset?
passages.english: whose (Nectarius') ordination, what order it observed, we do not see. But on the other hand, what wealth of matter, what elegance of words joined with weight of thought [there is] in that letter which Ambrose truly wrote to Theodosius for this very reason in the name of the council of Aquileia! Let the reader compare the two with each other himself, and judge by his own judgement whether in both [the letters] can seem to have been produced by the same hand. What, finally, [of the fact] that the author of this Italian letter seems to be ignorant of the agreement that had been sworn between Meletius and Paulinus, and which had restored concord to the Church of Antioch, although this was very well known to Ambrose?
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence, continuing a list of stylistic faults. "in utraque ab eadem manu prolecta videri possit" is grammatically awkward; it is taken as "whether [the letters] can seem to have been produced (prolecta, perhaps for producta or profecta) by the same hand", with "an" understood.

passages.original: Nam primo, tantum abest ut Orientales convicium sibi factum putaverint anno 382, quo ad illud concilium evocati sunt, ut ob hoc potius Occidentalium charita- tem laudaverint in litteris ad eos scriptis : deinde illi se ad Romanum concilium non solum Damasi, sed etiam Theodosii litteris vocatos aiunt, quod Hiero- nymus etiam asseruit (c). Qui itaque fieri potest, ut Theodosius ea tunc Ambrosio scripserit, quae Tille- montius, Fleurius et Cellerius aliique opinantur et fingunt? Postremo, Theodosius ipse scribere Ambro- sio haec minime potuit ante annum 382 jam inclina- tum : necesse itaque est, ut fatearis, hanc ipsam Am- brosii epistolam;
passages.english: For first, so far were the Easterners from thinking that an insult had been done to them in the year 382, when they were summoned to that council, that on this account they rather praised the charity of the Westerners in the letter written to them. Next, they say that they were called to the Roman council not only by a letter of Damasus but also by one of Theodosius, which Jerome also asserted (c). How, then, can it be that Theodosius at that time wrote to Ambrose the things that Tillemont, Fleury, Ceillier and others suppose and invent? Finally, Theodosius himself could by no means have written these things to Ambrose before the year 382 was already well advanced. It is necessary, therefore, that you admit that this very letter of Ambrose
passages.notes: The passage ends mid-sentence; it continues in the following text ("...was given at the very end of that year"). (c) is a footnote mark. "Cellerius" is taken to be Rémi Ceillier.
